sources.title: Trương Vĩnh Ký (Q655563), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-13): English label 'Pétrus Ky', Vietnamese label Trương Vĩnh Ký, English description 'Vietnamese scholar (1837-1898)', instance of human, born 1837-12-06, died 1898-09-01, occupations including linguist and journalist, no Korean label. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Phạm Thị Kim Ngân, 'Trương Vĩnh Ký và những đóng góp cho nền văn học và báo chí Việt Nam' (Truong Vinh Ky and his contributions to Vietnamese literature and journalism), Journal of Educational Equipment: Applied Research, vol. 2, no. 319, August 2024 (Vietnamese; read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: presents him as an erudite intellectual who left over 100 works and whose main contributions were writing, translating and publishing literature in quoc ngu (Latin-script Vietnamese) and founding quoc ngu journalism; describes his translations of Confucian texts and his transcriptions of Nom works (Kim Van Kieu, Luc Van Tien, Phan Tran), and his prose Chuyen doi xua and Chuyen di Bac ky nam At Hoi; says the Gia Dinh bao, handed to him by Admiral Ohier on 16 September 1869 (given as 1969 in the text), changed from a translation of the Courrier de Saigon into a paper with simple language, research pieces, proverbs, poems and tales, with Ton Tho Tuong, Huynh Tinh Cua and Truong Minh Ky as collaborators; notes his service on education and municipal councils and at the Hue court and that he was attacked as a French agent but is now more often assessed as a scholar. Secondary scholarly article, openly sympathetic, leaning on quoted assessments by Thanh Lang, Nguyen Van Trung and Trinh Van Thao.

Tim Doling, 'What Does the Future Hold for Petrus Ky's Mausoleum and Memorial House?', Saigoneer, 13 April 2015 (read in full). Heritage-writer article: trained first for the priesthood and worked in the early 1860s as an interpreter for the Paris Foreign Missions Society; later professor of oriental languages at the Collège des Interprètes, the École normale and the Collège des administrateurs stagiaires in Saigon; said to be fluent in at least ten languages; left over 100 works on literature, history and geography and grammar books on Chinese, Khmer, Lao, Malay, Siamese, Cham, Burmese, Tamil and Hindustani; edited the academic journal Miscellanées; the house he built in 1861; the 1927 statue and the 1935-37 mausoleum. Independent of the Vietnamese-language sources, but an article about a heritage site, partly relying on reputation.

Tuyết Nhi, 'How the 1st Quoc Ngu Newspaper Shaped the Foundation of Vietnam's Modern Journalism', Saigoneer (read in full). Heritage-history article: the French authorities chose quoc ngu as a bridge to the population and to train interpreters; the first Gia Dinh bao issue appeared on 15 April 1865 under the French interpreter Ernest Potteaux and mostly carried decrees; under Truong Vinh Ky's editorship in 1869 it diversified into articles, commentary, research, folklore, social reform and advertisements and gave the local intelligentsia a voice; although it served the colonial government's propaganda needs, the Vietnamese scholars running it turned it into a platform for quoc ngu and local culture; quotes the researcher Nguyen Hai Loc that French motives were not goodwill but that the accomplishment of Ky, Huynh Tinh Cua and Truong Minh Ky is visible in the paper. Journalism-history article; the closest thing here to a critical framing of the paper's origins.

'T'oung Pao va Ai tu ve Petrus Truong Vinh Ky' (T'oung Pao and the obituary of Petrus Truong Vinh Ky), Dac San Petrus Truong Vinh Ky, 2013, Toan Cau Hoi Ngo, pp. 51-55 (Petrus Ky alumni association magazine, Vietnamese; read in full). Translated excerpts from the 1899-1900 obituary in the Orientalist journal T'oung Pao by its editor Henri Cordier, including the eulogy read at the grave on 6 September 1898 by the native councillor Tran Ba Tho (he learned French early and used it in French service, taught future administrators at the Collège des administrateurs stagiaires alongside Philastre and Luro, helped spread quoc ngu by translating the main Vietnamese and Chinese authors, was still concerned in his last days with publishing his final works including a translation of Littré's dictionary) and Cordier's own survey: primers, Tam tu kinh and the Four Books in quoc ngu of which only the Great Learning, Doctrine of the Mean and part of Mencius were printed (Cordier does not know why the rest was stopped by the authorities), small works on the history and geography of Cochinchina, and many short articles, mostly in quoc ngu without French or Chinese translation. Contemporary but by a colonial-era orientalist and a pupil, reproduced in a community magazine for the school's alumni; admiring.

Milton E. Osborne, 'Truong Vinh Ky and Phan Thanh Gian: The Problem of a Nationalist Interpretation of 19th Century Vietnamese History', The Journal of Asian Studies, 1970 (Cambridge Core; ABSTRACT ONLY read, article body behind a paywall): says historians in Hanoi judged nineteenth-century figures by whether they resisted the French and condemned both men for not working against the French, whereas Saigon historians were more ready to consider sympathetically the factors that led to their choices. Counter-voice on how he has been judged; no behavioural claims drawn from it.

'Trương Vĩnh Ký - một nhân vật đa diện' (Truong Vinh Ky, a many-sided figure), DoanhNhan+ (Vietnamese; 13 September 2020; read in full): report on a symposium of the Vietnam Press Museum on 11 September 2020 at which historians and journalists describe him as a patriot in his own way who called on people to keep Vietnamese culture in a time of transition, citing his publication of Luc Van Tien by an anti-French author, a Vietnamese-history section in the Gia Dinh bao and his Chuyen di Bac ky of 1876 (once read as an intelligence report, now as a travel narrative); the researcher Lai Nguyen An says he is the largest and richest quoc ngu author since the script came into use and that critics often look only at his cooperation with the French; the chair concludes he is a many-sided figure needing several disciplines. Symposium report by participants largely defending him; used for how the record is contested.

Đoàn Lê Giang and Phạm Thị Tố Thy, 'Dịch văn học phương Tây ở Sài Gòn - Gia Định trong buổi bình minh của văn học quốc ngữ' (Translating Western literature in Saigon-Gia Dinh at the dawn of quoc ngu literature), Thu Dau Mot University Journal of Science, no. 4(29), 2016 (Vietnamese; read in full). Literary-history article: notes that his main effort was collecting and recording Vietnamese literature and working on language and learning, but that in his periodical Miscellanées (Thong loai khoa trinh, renamed Su loai thong khao from issue 2 in June 1889) he also printed two translations, a series of Western humorous stories and the Life of Aesop (from May 1889), the first such translations in the country by the authors' account; says the periodical's name marks it as a course of study by topic and that its opening words justify the fun by saying much teaching material becomes dull; the periodical later stopped. Independent literary-history article about translation, not a biography.

Angkor Database, 'Vinh Ky [Petrus Ky] Truong' author entry (read in full; short academic-database biography): born 6 December 1837 in Vinh Long and died 1 September 1898 in Saigon; after his father's death at nine grew up among French Catholic missionaries; studied Latin and modern languages at the Pinhalu school in Cambodia and then at Penang Seminary; interpreter for the Vietnamese delegation led by Phan Thanh Gian to Paris in 1863, also visiting Egypt, Spain, Portugal and Italy; first Vietnamese scholar to publish in European publications (notably the Bulletin de la Société de Géographie de Paris); author of Histoire d'Annam, described as the first significant history of Vietnam in a European language following European historiographic models; his publications helped popularise quoc ngu before its officialisation. Reference-style entry without citations.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_ky_doling, src_ky_kimngan, src_ky_cordier, src_ky_tdm | 1860s-1890s | heritage article, scholarly article, contemporary obituary, literary-history article] The sources describe grammars and teaching works across Chinese, Khmer, Lao, Malay, Siamese, Cham, Burmese, Tamil and Hindustani (Doling), translations of Chinese classics and transcriptions of Nom poems into quoc ngu (Kim Ngan, Cordier), small works on the history and geography of Cochinchina and many short articles (Cordier), and a periodical that carried Western humorous tales and the Life of Aesop (Doan Le Giang). The range is documented in separate works; none of the sources describes how he moved between fields, and much of the language work lies close to his post as an interpreter and teacher. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.54 to 66 / 0.50 because the range rests on lists of works in reference-style sources.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_ky_kimngan, src_ky_gdb, src_ky_tdm, src_ky_cordier | 1869-1889 | scholarly article, journalism-history article, literary-history article, contemporary obituary] After taking over the Gia Dinh bao he turned it from a translated official bulletin into a paper with research pieces, proverbs and tales in plain language, aimed at giving readers general knowledge (Kim Ngan, Saigoneer); his 1888-89 periodical was framed as a course of study with entertainment added to hold readers (Doan Le Giang); the obituary says he spread quoc ngu through translations. The aims are inferred from his publishing choices and from later authors' summaries, and the colonial government's own motives for backing the paper are a separate matter (Saigoneer). SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.50 to 62 / 0.46 because the claim about his aim leans on later admiring and defending accounts and one quoted literary historian.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_ky_kimngan, src_ky_gdb, src_ky_tdm, src_ky_doling | 1869-1889 | scholarly article, journalism-history article, literary-history article, heritage article] Given charge of the Gia Dinh bao in 1869 (1868 in some accounts), he and his co-workers added research, commentary, folklore and a wider range of content to a paper that had been mainly decrees (Kim Ngan, Saigoneer); two decades later he edited and published his own periodical Miscellanees (Doling, Doan Le Giang), which was later stopped. The change at the Gia Dinh bao was made inside a post assigned by the governor, and sources differ on the date and on how much was his own doing against his team's. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.50 to 62 / 0.48 because the 1869 post was assigned and the sources credit a team.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_ky_cordier, src_ky_doling, src_ky_angkor | 1850s-1898 | contemporary obituary, heritage article, reference entry] The eulogy read at his grave says he threw himself into a complete command of French from youth and was still occupied in his last days with publishing his final works, including a translation of Littre's dictionary; the other sources describe formal study at Pinhalu and Penang and grammars of many languages. The pursuit of depth is documented mainly by a pupil's eulogy in a colonial-era obituary, and the sources do not describe his methods. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.50 strong_inference to 60 / 0.44 inference because the single behavioural account is a graveside eulogy reproduced by an alumni magazine.

persistence.rationale: [src_ky_cordier, src_ky_kimngan, src_ky_doling | 1863-1898 | contemporary obituary, scholarly article, heritage article] The scholarly article says he published books from the age of 26 until his death, and the eulogy describes him still working on publication at the end; Cordier adds that some of his Four Books translations were blocked by the authorities and only part reached print. The work continued over decades, but the sources report outputs and do not describe how he handled obstacles. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.46 to 58 / 0.42 because the continuity is shown by publication lists and one eulogy.

collaboration.rationale: [src_ky_kimngan, src_ky_gdb, src_ky_cordier | 1869-1898 | scholarly article, journalism-history article, contemporary obituary] The Gia Dinh bao under his charge drew on Ton Tho Tuong, Huynh Tinh Cua and Truong Minh Ky (Kim Ngan, Saigoneer), and the eulogy says the administrators he trained alongside Philastre and Luro remained his friends. The collaborations are named but not described, and the training role is only reported by a pupil. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 58 / 0.44 strong_inference to 56 / 0.40 inference because the named partners are not documented in action.

adaptability.rationale: [src_ky_doling, src_ky_angkor, src_ky_kimngan | 1850s-1880s | heritage article, reference entry, scholarly article] He moved between missionary schools in Cambodia and Penang, work as an interpreter, teaching posts, editing and, per the scholarly article, councils and a brief role at the Hue court. The change of roles is documented, but whether it reflects adjustment or the opportunities open to him is not discussed, and the same bridging between institutions is also what later critics have read as political dependence (Osborne abstract, Saigoneer). SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 60 / 0.44 to 56 / 0.40 and impact marked dual-edged because the sources do not separate adaptability from circumstance.

portrait.source: Halftone portrait of Trương Vĩnh Ký (photographer or original maker not named) printed on page 61 of 'Đông Dương ngày xưa và ngày nay' (L'Indochine d'hier et d'aujourd'hui) by Henri Cucherousset, translated by Vũ Công Nghị (Hanoi, 1926), with the printed bilingual caption 'Un savant Cochinchinois : Pétrus Truong-Vinh-Ky / Một nhà bác-học Nam-kỳ : Ông Pétrus Trương-Vĩnh-Ký'. The book is digitised on Gallica (ark bpt6k6151241r; Gallica item record rights field 'domaine public'). The image file is the Wikimedia Commons extract of that page (1862 x 2609) downscaled to 642 x 900 with no upscaling; the caption is not part of the crop and was read in the book's PDF page.
portrait.license: Public domain: published in Hanoi in 1926 (before 1931, so public domain in the United States); the maker of the portrait is not named and the digitising library's item record states 'public domain'
portrait.attribution: Unnamed maker, portrait of Pétrus Trương Vĩnh Ký, plate in Henri Cucherousset, Đông Dương ngày xưa và ngày nay (Hanoi, 1926), p. 61; digitised by the Bibliothèque nationale de France (Gallica).
portrait.creator: Unknown (reproduced in Cucherousset / Vũ Công Nghị, Hanoi 1926)

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (lead) / REPLACED: the lead's Commons 'Petrus Truong Vinh Ky 1883' (Gallica, BnF Société de Géographie) did not survive. The BnF OAI record for ark btv1b84509187 (read via the Gallica OAIRecord service) is titled '[Joannes Baptistus Petrus Truong-Vinh-Ky]', dated 1883, shelfmark SG PORTRAIT-1008, and states 'restricted use (convention Société de géographie)', which contradicts Commons' PD-Art/PD-old-70 label; the Gallica item page itself returned a Cloudflare challenge (bot wall, not bypassed), so the restriction was read from the OAI record. Separately, the sitter in that 1883 print looks distinctly younger than a man of 45 and unlike the other portraits, so identity is also doubtful; it was not used. Other leads rejected: musée du quai Branly PP0021911 is a photograph of a 1889 bust by Sylvain Raffegaud (a sculpture, holder rights not checked); the Arnoux/Gsell 'Voyage de l'Egypte à l'Indochine' extract is identified only by a content-farm blog. REPLACEMENT: the 1926 halftone plate in Cucherousset, 'Đông Dương ngày xưa và ngày nay' p. 61, whose printed caption (bilingual) names him; I read the caption on the book's PDF page rendered from the Commons copy of the Gallica scan, and the Gallica item record for the book (bpt6k6151241r) says 'domaine public'. Gallica's page images then returned bot-wall 403 and were not retried. Rights basis: published in Hanoi in 1926, before 1931, so public domain in the US; the portrait's maker and the date of the underlying photograph are unknown. KIND: likeness, with a caveat that the plate is a 1926 halftone of an undated image, so it is not stated whether it reproduces a lifetime photograph or a drawing; the face and dress (decorations, court dress) are consistent with other portraits of him in later life that were viewed. Image quality is coarse (halftone, no enhancement). PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE (2026-11-13, Wikidata API) Q655563, label 'Pétrus Ky' (en), Trương Vĩnh Ký (vi), description 'Vietnamese scholar (1837-1898)', human, born 1837-12-06, died 1898-09-01, no Korean label. REGION south_asia (repo precedent codes Southeast Asia as south_asia: ho-xuan-huong, ho-chi-minh, jose-rizal, kartini, tan-kah-kee; confirmed, there is no Southeast Asia id). ERA 19th_century. Nationality VN. KO NAME 쯔엉빈끼: Wikidata and the Korean Wikipedia have no entry, so this is the researcher's transcription following the repo's unspaced style for Vietnamese names (호쑤언흐엉); a human Korean check is advisable. SCOPE: scored on scholarly, linguistic, editorial and teaching conduct only; his service with the French colonial administration (interpreter, education and municipal councils, the Hue mission, Gia Dinh bao under the colonial governor) is context, noted in rows only as a limit on what can be inferred, and the contested assessment is carried by the Osborne abstract, the DoanhNhan+ symposium report and the Saigoneer article. VOCABULARY: occupations scholar, teacher, editor; fields linguistics, education, literature; tags polymath, communicator, cross_disciplinary; archetypes cross_disciplinary_generalist, scholarly_specialist; impact domains cultural, educational, literary. ATTRIBUTION: attributable (dated publications, posts and a periodical he edited). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Pham Thi Kim Ngan 2024 (src_ky_kimngan). READ (8 sources besides Wikidata): Kim Ngan 2024 (full), Doling/Saigoneer 2015 (full), Saigoneer Gia Dinh bao article (full), Cordier obituary excerpts in the 2013 alumni magazine (full), Osborne 1970 (abstract only), DoanhNhan+ 2020 report (full), Doan Le Giang and Pham Thi To Thy 2016 (full), Angkor Database entry (full). Wikipedia (English) read for orientation only and not cited; a Wikipedia statement that he was 'professor of French' and 'appointed to Hue in 1876' is not used. Britannica and historicvietnam.com were blocked (403 bot wall) and not read. Not opened: Bouchot 1927 biography, Nguyen Dinh Dau 'Petrus Ky - Noi oan the ky', Osborne article body, Ky's own autobiographical manuscripts, any of his own works. PERSPECTIVES: (1) Vietnamese scholarly secondary literature (Kim Ngan, Doan Le Giang); (2) English-language heritage and journalism writing (Doling, Saigoneer); (3) contemporary colonial-orientalist obituary and pupil eulogy (Cordier via the alumni magazine); (4) historiographic counter-voice on nationalist judgement (Osborne abstract); (5) symposium report defending him (DoanhNhan+). NON-SELF BEHAVIOURAL SOURCES: Kim Ngan, Doan Le Giang, Doling, Saigoneer, Cordier (his own letters and diaries not used). ADVERSARIAL SOURCE: none found; the critical Hanoi-school readings appear only second-hand (Osborne abstract, DoanhNhan+, Kim Ngan). CONTRADICTIONS AND LIMITS: Gia Dinh bao handover dated 16 September 1869 (Kim Ngan, with a typo giving 1969), 1868 by other accounts; 'fluent in at least ten languages' (Doling) versus 26 languages in popular pieces (not used); the Wikipedia summary of his career differs on dates. Sparse 7-row profile by design: no creative_originality row (the 'first prose writer' claims come from quoted literary historians), no curiosity row (the breadth is carried by cross_domain_range), and no rows for his French-state roles. MAJOR ACHIEVEMENT GATE: cards (1) quoc ngu transcription and translation of Vietnamese and Chinese texts, (2) Gia Dinh bao, (3) his language and teaching works and publication in European venues.
